item.description:
📚 Physics News
Scientists at Rutgers and in Estonia have used invisible light to look into tiny magnetic whirlpools, called vortices, inside a superconductor, revealing details that could help researchers develop better materials for carrying electricity.

item.title: Machine learning helps track semiconductor defects under more realistic temperature conditions
item.description:
📚 Physics News
All materials contain inherent defects. These are not always harmful, since they can be used to engineer and introduce certain properties into a material. However, it is crucial to understand how they function and how they affect the material's properties.

item.title: Electrical signals reveal hidden magnetic information in altermagnets for first time
item.description:
📚 Physics News
Researchers have experimentally demonstrated, for the first time, that it is possible to obtain from an altermagnet a spin current that can transport magnetic information. This result is supported by the theoretical model of electron transport developed by the CFM group. Altermagnets are a new class of materials that, despite not exhibiting the net magnetization characteristic of conventional magnets, can generate this type of current.

Quantum key distribution (QKD) is evolving toward large-scale metropolitan networks that interoperate with modern communication infrastructures. Although wavelength division multiplexing (WDM) architectures hold great promise for high secure-key throughput and multi-user access, existing implementations suffer from security vulnerabilities introduced by trusted nodes, limited topological flexibility, and high resource overhead. Here, we experimentally demonstrate a flexible and resource-efficient mode-pairing QKD network enabled by integrated photonics, which natively supports trusted-node-free networking. item.title: Mastering Baghchal by Self-Play with Deep Reinforcement Learning
item.description:
📚 Preprints
👤 Ranjit Raut, Aarav Subedi, Sagun Rai
Baghchal is a two-player asymmetric board game of Nepali origin. In the gameplay, four tigers attempt to capture goats while twenty goats seek to immobilize the tigers. Baghchal has received limited attention in the deep reinforcement learning (RL) literature despite its strategic complexity, perfect information structure, and cultural significance. We present a systematic investigation of four deep reinforcement learning algorithms, viz. Deep Q-Network (DQN), REINFORCE, Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), and MuZero. These algorithms are applied to both sides of asymmetric gameplay through self-play training in Baghchal. Each of these algorithms is evaluated in terms of win rate, draw rate, average captures, training convergence, and computational cost. In our experimental results, MuZer…

item.title: Ultrathin metal layer boosts spin-related signals, opening a door to ultralow-power electronics
item.description:
📚 Physics News
Researchers at Kyushu University have found that an ultrathin layer of iridium manganese (IrMn) can improve two spin-related signals in a structure made of a magnetic insulator and a platinum film. By examining how spin currents are generated and absorbed, the team gained insights into how the intermediate layer improves spin transfer. The findings could inform the development of ultralow-power devices for computing and energy harvesting.

item.description:
📚 Preprints
👤 Nsini Ignatius Udo
Centrifugal pumps working in saline environments directly bridge corrosion-related material deterioration, dynamic response and hydraulic efficiency domains, yet condition-monitoring approaches often isolate these. A preceding work by the author introduced a Pump Degradation Index (PDI) by combining a corrosion-related material degradation indicator derived from coupons, RMS vibration and hydraulic-efficiency degradation into one condition indicator. This work explores the potential to link these by proposing a time-based, physics-based digital twin framework where the PDI is used as a transparent intermediate state of degradation rather than as a failure probability or end-of-life indicator. Five layers are used: physical asset and sensing; data processing and classification; normalized…

The commemoration of the 150th anniversary of Ildefons Cerdà’s death during the Cerdà Year 2026, together with Barcelona’s designation as World Capital of Architecture 2026, provides a timely context in which to reassess the contemporary relevance of Cerdà’s urban principles. This study examines whether the spatial organisation of food retail in the Eixample district continues to reflect the proximity-based and territorially balanced provision envisaged in his plan. Using georeferenced data for seven food retail categories, we combine kernel intensity estimation, Clark–Evans statistics, inhomogeneous Ripley’s K-functions, entropy measures across Voronoi-based market catchments, and inhomogeneous Poisson point process models. item.description:

👤 Hong Jin Fan, Zefang Yang, Yuhang Liu, Jinchi Li, Lin Liu, Yifeng Wang 等12位作者
Aqueous manganese batteries based on MnO2 electrodeposition-dissolution process offer a compelling route to safe, low-cost and scalable energy storage. Despite their merits of high specific capacity and voltage, the hindrance towards practical implementation is the parasitic reaction and accumulation of dead manganese, leading to poor reversibility and low energy efficiency. Here, we identify the lattice-oxygen topology as the structural origin of Mn3+-driven parasitic reaction during weakly acidic MnO2 dissolution. By synthesizing a series of MnO2 polymorphs with a controllable transition from pyramidal (Opy) to planar oxygen (Opl) topology, we reveal that the rapid Opy dissolution accounts for the formation of MnOOH intermediates (i.e., Mn3+), but MnOOH is suppressed on Opl-dominated pa…

item.title: Theoretical method uses light to locate anyons, potential quantum computing building blocks
item.description:
📚 Physics News
Theoretical physicists at Emory University have discovered a way to use light to detect the "spectral fingerprints" of anyons—exotic quasiparticles that emerge from the collective behavior of many electrons. Their findings are published in Physical Review Letters. The work offers a new tool for the study of anyons, which hold potential as fundamental building blocks for quantum computing.

👤 Jakob Nyberg, Sandor Berglund, Andrei Buhaiu, Joakim Loxdal, Pontus Johnson, Mathias Ekstedt
We have developed the MAL Simulator, a cyber operation simulator based on the Meta Attack Language (MAL). The MAL Simulator is intended for decision-driven cyber attack and defense simulations, for system analysis and the development of automated agents. By building the simulator around an attack modeling language, it can be adapted to different target domains without modifying the source code. We used the simulator for two case studies where we trained two types of agents for automated cyber operations: a defensive agent and an offensive agent. To ground the experiments, we base the models in data collected from an emulated network implemented in the cyber range CRATE. Tactile alerts can communicate spatial and temporal information in automo-tive human–machine interfaces while reducing reliance on visual and auditory channels. Evidence on appropriate body locations for such alerts remains dis-tributed across automotive human-machine interface (HMI), haptic-interface, and somatosensory research. This study examines how body location may influ-ence the perception and processing of tactile alerts in driving contexts. It adopts a sequential evidence-to-consensus design comprising a scoping review of automo-tive HMI studies, reported in accordance with PRISMA-ScR; an umbrella review of systematic reviews and meta-analyses on tactile perception and processing; and a modified Delphi study with six specialists from automotive industry, design, and neuroscience.…

While their integration can significantly enhance systemic robustness, network topologies and governance models differ drastically between Air and HSR networks across regions. Using a multi-layer network representation of scheduled services, topological metrics and a schedule-based routing algorithm, the networks are subjected to simulated random airport failures, adaptive targeted hub attacks, and operational airline shutdowns. Direct air capture requires sorbents that bind CO2 selectively yet release it with low energy. Bis-iminoguanidines capture CO2 by crystallizing as hydrated carbonate salts, but the molecular events linking water loss, proton transfer, and CO2 release remain unresolved. Here we combine variable-temperature single-crystal neutron and X-ray diffraction with ab initio molecular dynamics to determine how two crystalline carbonate phases follow different regeneration pathways. We show that lattice water acts as a molecular gate for carbonate protonation. In a metastable phase, water is isolated from carbonate, creating a softer hydrogen-bond network that promotes surface proton transfer and a transient carbonic-acid configuration. Conventional slope protection systems are susceptible to runoff-induced erosion, surface-soil loss, and shallow soil deformation under rainfall conditions. This study developed a Y-shaped bamboo structure integrating runoff interception and seepage drainage functions. Model tests and theoretical analysis were conducted to investigate the runoff interception efficiency of the structure under simulated rainfall conditions. Hyperspectral imaging (HSI) captures rich, wavelength-dependent information linked to mineralised tissue composition, while3D reconstruction preserves surface morphology and structural detail. Combining the two offers a powerful, non-contactapproach for bone assessment, yet existing hyperspectral 3D reconstruction methods rely on externally estimated cameraposes (e.g., via COLMAP), an assumption that is often unreliable on bone surfaces due to their low texture, specular reflectance,and irregular morphology. item.title: Slow-motion electron camera reveals light-driven quantum jumps in graphene
item.description:

Using a new slow-motion electron camera, physicists from Regensburg, Marburg and Jülich revealed how intense electric fields drive electrons in graphene, causing them to jump across energy gaps in a seemingly paradoxical manner. This was made possible by a novel combination of laser technology and electron microscopy.

item.title: Hybrid mechanics of coupled qubits
item.description:
📚 The Journal of Chemical Physics Current Issue
We find that a technique analogous to hybrid mechanics previously developed for Gaussian coherent states and molecular vibrations, can be extended to SU(2) coherent states describing coupled qubits. This formulation reveals a sparse structure of the propagator, leading to a computationally efficient scheme while maintaining numerical accuracy. As a result, the method enables simulations of larger qubit systems on classical computers. In particular, we demonstrate accurate real-time propagation for systems of up to 21 qubits, which would be computationally demanding using straightforward quantum-dynamics approaches.

item.title: SPINE: A machine-learning program is on the trail of ghost particles
item.description:
📚 Physics News
Neutrinos are among the most abundant particles in the universe, but they are also among the most elusive. Nearly massless, they are produced by nuclear reactions in the sun, exploding stars, particle accelerators and even the decay of radioactive elements on Earth. They interact so weakly with ordinary matter that trillions pass through each person every second without leaving a trace. Studying these ghostly particles could help answer some of the biggest questions in physics, from the nature of dark matter to why matter exists at all.

item.title: Can gravitational fields break and reconnect? Einstein's equations suggest they can
item.description:
📚 Physics News
More than a century after Einstein first devised the equations that describe gravity, physicists are still finding new ways of interpreting them. Luca Comisso, an associate research scientist in Columbia University's departments of Astronomy and Physics and the Columbia Astrophysics Laboratory, and Felipe A. Asenjo of Universidad Adolfo Ibáñez in Chile, recently found a new way of looking at Einstein's equations that reveals a striking analogy with "magnetic reconnection" in plasmas, which occurs when magnetic field lines break and reconnect, powering explosive phenomena such as solar flares.
